<!-- lem-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:Basis_Invariance}
Let $\mathbf X$ and $\mathbf Y$ be bases of $\mathfrak{g}$ related by $\mathbf Y=N\mathbf X$, with $N$ invertible.
With the state, representation and inner product fixed, the uncertainty defined in Eq.~\eqref{eq:MT_Lie_Uncertainty} satisfies $\mathcal{U}_\psi(\mathbf X)=\mathcal{U}_\psi(\mathbf Y)$.
<!-- end lem-1 -->
<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:Uncertainty_Conservation}
Within the weight space $V_{\Lambda,\mu}$ of an irreducible representation of $\mathfrak{g}$ with highest weight $\Lambda$, the Lie algebraic uncertainty is constant: 
every state $\ket{\psi_\mu}\in V_{\Lambda,\mu}$ satisfies
\begin{align}\label{eq:MT_Uncertainty_Conservation}
    \mathcal{U}_{\psi_\mu}(\mathfrak{g})
    =
    \langle C_2\rangle_{\psi_\mu}
    -
    \langle\mu,\mu\rangle,
\end{align}
where $\langle C_2\rangle_{\psi_\mu}$ is the expectation value of the quadratic Casimir element, and $\langle\mu,\mu\rangle$ is the squared norm of the weight $\mu$.
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- thm-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:Simple_Bound}
A complex simple Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ of rank $r$, acting in a finite-dimensional irreducible representation with highest weight $\Lambda=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i\omega_i$, satisfies
\begin{align}\label{eq:MT_Optimal_Uncertainty}
    \mathcal{U}_\psi(\mathfrak{g})
    \geqslant
    \vec{\lambda}^{\mathbf{T}}\cdot\vec{\xi},
\end{align}
for every quantum state $\psi$ in the representation space.
Here $\vec{\lambda}$ is the Dynkin coefficient vector and $\vec{\xi}\coloneqq C^{-1}\vec{\alpha}$, where $C$ is the Cartan matrix and $\vec{\alpha}$ collects the squared lengths of the simple roots.
The bound is optimal and is attained by a highest-weight state.
<!-- end thm-2 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:Semisimple_Bound}
A complex semisimple Lie algebra
$\mathfrak{g}=\bigoplus_{k=1}^{s}\mathfrak{g}_k$
with finite dimensional irreducible representation
$V(\Lambda)\simeq\bigotimes_{k=1}^{s}V_k(\Lambda_k)$
inherits its optimal uncertainty bound from $\mathfrak{g}_k$.
Writing $\vec{\lambda}^{(k)}$ for the Dynkin coefficient vector of $\Lambda_k$
and $\vec{\xi}^{(k)}$ for the corresponding algebraic coefficient vector associated with $\mathfrak{g}_k$,
every quantum state $\psi$ obeys
\begin{align}
\mathcal{U}_{\psi}(\mathfrak{g})
\geqslant
\sum_{k=1}^{s}
\bigl(\vec{\lambda}^{(k)}\bigr)^{\mathbf{T}}\vec{\xi}^{(k)}.
\end{align}
Equality is attained by a tensor product of highest-weight states, one for each $\mathfrak{g}_k$, establishing the optimality of the bound.
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- mydef-1: body_md -->
{Lie Algebra}{Lie_Algebra}
    A Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ over a field $\mathbb{F}= \mathbb{R}$ or  $\mathbb{C}$ is a vector space equipped with a bilinear operation $[\cdot,\cdot]:\mathfrak{g}\times\mathfrak{g}\to\mathfrak{g}$ referred to as the Lie bracket, which satisfies the following properties:
    \begin{itemize}
      \item \textbf{Anti-symmetry}. $[x,y]=-[y,x]$,
      \item \textbf{Jacobi Identity}. $[x,[y,z]]+[y,[z,x]]+[z,[x,y]]=0$,
    \end{itemize}
    for all $x$, $y$, and $z\in\mathfrak{g}$.
<!-- end mydef-1 -->
<!-- mydef-2: body_md -->
{Ideals}{Ideal}
A subspace $I\subseteq\mathfrak{g}$ is called an ideal of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ if it is invariant under the adjoint action of $\mathfrak{g}$, namely, if
\begin{align}
\mathrm{ad}_x[y]\coloneqq[x,y]\in I
\end{align}
for all $x\in\mathfrak{g}$ and $y\in I$.
In compact form, this condition is expressed as
\begin{align}
[\mathfrak{g},I]\subseteq I.
\end{align}
Thus, ideals characterize those subspaces preserved by the intrinsic adjoint structure of the Lie algebra.
<!-- end mydef-2 -->
<!-- mydef-3: body_md -->
{Solvable Lie algebras}{Solvable}
A Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ is called solvable if its derived series terminates after finitely many steps, namely, if there exists an integer $m\geqslant 1$ such that
\begin{align}
\mathfrak{g}^{(m)}=0.
\end{align}
<!-- end mydef-3 -->
<!-- mydef-4: body_md -->
{Simple Lie algebra}{Simple_Lie_Algebra}
A Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ is called simple if it is non-abelian and has no nontrivial ideals; that is, its only ideals are ${0}$ and $\mathfrak{g}$ itself.
<!-- end mydef-4 -->
<!-- mydef-5: body_md -->
{Semisimple Lie algebra}{Semisimple_Lie_Algebra}
A Lie algebra
$\mathfrak{g}$
is called semisimple if it decomposes into a direct sum of simple Lie algebras,
\begin{align}
    \mathfrak{g}
    =
    \bigoplus_k
    \mathfrak{g}_k ,
\end{align}
where each
$\mathfrak{g}_k$
is simple.
<!-- end mydef-5 -->
<!-- mydef-6: body_md -->
{Representation of a Lie Algebra}{repn_Lie_alg}
Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a Lie algebra over a field $\mathbb F$, with $V$ a vector space over $\mathbb F$. 
A representation of $\mathfrak{g}$ on $V$ is a linear, bracket-preserving map
\begin{align}
    \pi:\mathfrak{g}\to\mathfrak{gl}(V),
\end{align}
where $\mathfrak{gl}(V)$ is the Lie algebra of linear endomorphisms of $V$; equivalently,
\begin{align}
    \pi\left([x,y]\right)
    =
    [\pi(x),\pi(y)]
\end{align}
for all $x,y\in\mathfrak{g}$.
<!-- end mydef-6 -->
<!-- mydef-7: body_md -->
{Roots}{Roots}
Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and let $\mathfrak h^*$ denote the dual space of $\mathfrak h$. The adjoint action of $\mathfrak h$ decomposes $\mathfrak{g}$ into simultaneous eigenspaces. For each $\alpha\in\mathfrak h^*$, define
\begin{align}
    \mathfrak{g}_\alpha
    = \left\{x\in\mathfrak{g}
    \;\middle|\;
    \mathrm{ad}_h(x)=[h,x]=\alpha(h)x,
    \ \forall h\in\mathfrak h
    \right\}.
\end{align}
A nonzero functional $\alpha\in\mathfrak h^*$ for which $\mathfrak{g}_\alpha\neq\{0\}$ is called a root, and the collection of all such roots is denoted by $\Phi\subset\mathfrak h^*$. 
This gives the canonical root space decomposition
\begin{align}\label{eq:Root_Space_Decomposition}
    \mathfrak{g}
    =
    \underbrace{\mathfrak h}_{\text{Cartan Subalgebra}}
    \oplus
    \underbrace{
    \bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Phi}
    \mathfrak{g}_\alpha
    }_{\text{Root Space}}.
\end{align}
<!-- end mydef-7 -->
<!-- mydef-8: body_md -->
{Simple Roots}{Simple_Roots}
Let $\Phi$ be the root system of a complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$, and fix a choice of positive roots $\Phi^+$. 
A root $\alpha\in\Phi^+$ is called simple if it cannot be decomposed as a sum of two positive roots, i.e.,
\begin{align}
    \alpha\neq \beta+\gamma,
\end{align}
for all $\beta,\gamma\in\Phi^+$.
The set of all simple roots is denoted by
\begin{align}\label{eq:simple_roots_set}
    \Pi=\{\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r\},
\end{align}
where $r=\mathrm{rank}(\mathfrak{g})=\dim\mathfrak h$. 
Equivalently, $\Pi$ is the unique linearly independent subset of $\Phi^+$ such that every positive root is a non-negative integer linear combination of elements of $\Pi$.
<!-- end mydef-8 -->
<!-- mydef-9: body_md -->
{Special Linear Lie Algebra}{A_n}
The special linear Lie algebra of order $n$ over the field $\mathbb C$, denoted by
$\mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb C)$ or $\mathfrak{sl}(n,\mathbb C)$, is the Lie algebra consisting of all
$n\times n$ matrices with entries in $\mathbb C$ and vanishing trace. 
Explicitly,
\begin{align}
    \mathfrak{sl}(n,\mathbb C)
    \coloneqq
    \left\{
    X\in M_n(\mathbb C)
    \;\middle|\;
    \Tr[X]=0
    \right\},
\end{align}
equipped with the Lie bracket given by the matrix commutator; that is
\begin{align}
    [X,Y]=XY-YX.
\end{align}
<!-- end mydef-9 -->
<!-- mydef-10: body_md -->
{Odd-Dimensional Special Orthogonal Lie Algebra $B_n$}{B_n}
The odd-dimensional special orthogonal Lie algebra is the Lie algebra associated with the special orthogonal group in odd dimension.
Over the field $\mathbb C$, it is usually denoted by $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$ or $\mathfrak{so}(2n+1,\mathbb C)$ and is defined as the set of all $(2n+1)\times(2n+1)$ matrices that infinitesimally preserve a non-degenerate symmetric bilinear form. 
Equivalently, it can be written as
\begin{align}
\mathfrak{so}(2n+1,\mathbb C)
=
\left\{
X\in M_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)
\;\middle|\;
X^{T}S+SX=0
\right\},
\end{align}
where $S$ is the matrix representing the chosen symmetric bilinear form
\begin{align}
S=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0\\
0 & 0 & I_n\\
0 & I_n & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\end{align}
The Lie bracket is the usual matrix commutator.
<!-- end mydef-10 -->
<!-- mydef-11: body_md -->
{Symplectic Lie Algebra $C_n$}{C_n}
The symplectic Lie algebra is the Lie algebra consisting of all linear transformations that infinitesimally preserve a symplectic form.
Over the field $\mathbb C$, the symplectic Lie algebra is usually denoted by $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ or $\mathfrak{sp}(2n,\mathbb C)$.
It is defined as
\begin{align}
\mathfrak{sp}(2n,\mathbb C)
=
\left\{
X\in M_{2n}(\mathbb C)
\;\middle|\;
X^{T}S+SX=0
\right\},
\end{align}
where $S$ represents the standard symplectic form
\begin{align}
S=
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & I_n\\
-I_n & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\end{align}
<!-- end mydef-11 -->
<!-- mydef-12: body_md -->
{Even-Dimensional Special Orthogonal Lie Algebra $D_n$}{D_n}
The even-dimensional special orthogonal Lie algebra is the Lie algebra associated with the special orthogonal group in even dimension.
Over the field $\mathbb C$, it is usually denoted by $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ or $\mathfrak{so}(2n,\mathbb C)$ and is defined as 
\begin{align}
\mathfrak{so}(2n,\mathbb C)
=
\left\{
X\in M_{2n}(\mathbb C)
\;\middle|\;
X^{T}S+SX=0
\right\},
\end{align}
where $S$ stands for the following symmetric bilinear form
\begin{align}
S=
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & I_n\\
I_n & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\end{align}
<!-- end mydef-12 -->
<!-- mydef-13: body_md -->
{Killing Form}{Killing_Form}
For a finite-dimensional Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ over $\mathbb C$, the Killing form $\kappa_{\mathrm{Kill}}$ is the symmetric bilinear form 
\begin{align}
   \kappa_{\mathrm{Kill}}: \mathfrak{g}\times\mathfrak{g}\to\mathbb C,
\end{align}
defined by
\begin{align} \label{eq:Killing_form}
    \kappa_{\mathrm{Kill}}(x,y) \coloneqq 
    \Tr[\mathrm{ad}_x \mathrm{ad}_y], \qquad x,y\in\mathfrak{g}
\end{align}
where $\mathrm{ad}$ denotes the adjoint representation specified in Eq.~\eqref{eq:ad_rep}.
<!-- end mydef-13 -->
<!-- mydef-14: body_md -->
{Inner Product on $\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R}$}{Inner_product_alg}
Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a complex semisimple Lie algebra with compact real form $\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R}$, and let $\kappa$ be the normalized invariant bilinear form introduced in Eq.~\eqref{eq:normal_Killing}. 
Since $\kappa$ is negative definite on $\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R}$, it defines a positive-definite inner product by
\begin{align}\label{eq:Inner_product_algebra}
    (x,y)\coloneqq
    -\kappa(x,y), \qquad x, y \in \mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R}.
\end{align}
<!-- end mydef-14 -->
<!-- mylem-1: body_md -->
{Invariance of the Inner Product}{Invariance_Inner_Product}
The inner product $(\cdot,\cdot)$ defined in Eq.~\eqref{eq:Inner_product_algebra} satisfies
\begin{align}
    ([x,y],z)=(x,[y,z])
\end{align}
for all $x,y,z\in\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R}$.
<!-- end mylem-1 -->
<!-- mylem-2: body_md -->
{Killing Form Identification}{Killing_Form_Identification}
Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and let $\kappa$ be the normalized invariant bilinear form in Eq.~\eqref{eq:normal_Killing} on $\mathfrak{g}$ whose restriction to $\mathfrak h$ is nondegenerate. 
Then each functional
$\alpha\in\mathfrak h^*$ determines a unique element
$t_\alpha\in\mathfrak h$ such that
\begin{align}\label{eq:roots_action_KF}
    \alpha(h)
    =
    \kappa(t_\alpha,h),
    \qquad
    \forall\,h\in\mathfrak h .
\end{align}
<!-- end mylem-2 -->
<!-- mydef-15: body_md -->
{Induced Bilinear Form and Root-Space Inner Product}{Inner_Product_Root_Space}
For elements $\alpha,\beta\in\mathfrak h^*$, we define the induced bilinear form by
\begin{align} \label{eq:Inner_root}
\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle
\coloneqq
\kappa(t_\alpha,t_\beta)
\end{align}
where $t_\alpha,t_\beta\in\mathfrak h$ are the unique elements associated with $\alpha$ and $\beta$ (see Lem.~\ref{lem:Killing_Form_Identification}) through the normalized invariant bilinear form in Eq.~\eqref{eq:normal_Killing}.
<!-- end mydef-15 -->
<!-- mydef-16: body_md -->
{Dual Basis of the Cartan Subalgebra $\mathfrak h$}{Dual_Basis_Cartan_Subalgebra}
Let $\mathfrak h$ be a Cartan subalgebra equipped with the normalized invariant bilinear form $\kappa(\cdot,\cdot)$ defined in Eq.~\eqref{eq:normal_Killing}.
Given a basis $\{h_i\}_{i=1}^r$ of $\mathfrak h$, its $\kappa$-dual basis $\{h^i\}_{i=1}^r$ is defined by
\begin{align}
    \kappa(h_i,h^j)
    =
    \delta_{ij}.
\end{align}
<!-- end mydef-16 -->
<!-- mylem-3: body_md -->
{Dual Basis Expression of the Induced Bilinear Form}{Dual_Basis_Contraction}
For $\alpha,\beta\in\mathfrak h^*$, the induced bilinear form $\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle$ admits the following representation
\begin{align}\label{eq:dual_basis_general}
    \langle\alpha,\beta\rangle
    =
    \sum_{i=1}^r
    \alpha(h_i)\beta(h^i).
\end{align}
Here $\{h_i\}_{i=1}^r$ is a Cartan basis
and $\{h^i\}_{i=1}^r$ is $\kappa$-dual basis (see Def.~\ref{def:Dual_Basis_Cartan_Subalgebra}),  with $\kappa$ normalized as in Eq.~\eqref{eq:normal_Killing}.
On the real root space, setting $\alpha=\beta\in E$, Eq.~\eqref{eq:dual_basis_general} induces the associated squared norm
\begin{align}
\label{eq:dual_basis_norm}
    \|\alpha\|^2
    \coloneqq
    \langle\alpha,\alpha\rangle
    =
    \sum_{i=1}^r
    \alpha(h_i)\alpha(h^i).
\end{align}
<!-- end mylem-3 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Using the Killing form identification of Lem.~\ref{lem:Killing_Form_Identification}, we have
\begin{align}
    \alpha(h)&=\kappa(t_\alpha,h),\\
    \beta(h)&=\kappa(t_\beta,h),
\end{align}
for every $h\in\mathfrak h$.
This allows the right-hand side of Eq.~\eqref{eq:dual_basis_general} to be expressed as
\begin{align}\label{eq:DBP_RHS}
    \sum_{i=1}^r\alpha(h_i)\beta(h^i)
    =
    \sum_{i=1}^r\kappa(t_\alpha,h_i)\kappa(t_\beta,h^i)
    =
    \kappa\left(t_\alpha,\sum_{i=1}^r\kappa(t_\beta,h^i)h_i\right).
\end{align}
Since the $\kappa$-dual basis $\{h^i\}_{i=1}^r$ also forms a basis of the Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, with expansion coefficients determined by the Killing form, we further have
\begin{align}
    t_{\beta}=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\kappa(t_\beta,h^i)h_i.
\end{align}
Substituting this relation into Eq.~\eqref{eq:DBP_RHS}, we arrive at
\begin{align}
    \sum_{i=1}^r\alpha(h_i)\beta(h^i)
    =
    \kappa\left(t_\alpha,t_\beta\right)
    =
    \langle\alpha,\beta\rangle,
\end{align}
which completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- mydef-17: body_md -->
{Weyl Vector}{Weyl_Vector}
Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a complex semisimple Lie algebra, and fix a choice of positive roots $\Phi^+$. 
The Weyl vector is defined as the half-sum of all positive roots:
\begin{align}\label{eq:weyl_vector1}
\delta 
\coloneqq 
\frac12 \sum_{\alpha \in \Phi^+} \alpha \in \mathfrak h^*.
\end{align}
<!-- end mydef-17 -->
<!-- mydef-18: body_md -->
{Chevalley Basis}{Chevalley_Basis}
Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a complex semisimple Lie algebra of rank $r$, with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$
and root system $\Phi$.
After fixing a set of positive roots $\Phi^+\subset\Phi$,
the associated Chevalley basis takes the form
\begin{align}
    \{ h_i,
    e_\alpha,
    f_\alpha
    \mid
    i=1,\dots,r,\,
    \alpha\in\Phi^+\},
\end{align}
Here the rank is $r=\dim\mathfrak h$, the elements $h_i=h_{\alpha_i}$ for the simple roots $\alpha_i$ form a basis of $\mathfrak h$, while $e_{\alpha}$  and $f_{\alpha}$ span the root spaces associated with $\alpha$ and $-\alpha$ respectively.
In particular, they satisfy
\begin{align}
    [h_i,e_\alpha]= \alpha(h_i)e_\alpha,
    \quad     
    [h_i,f_\alpha]= -\alpha(h_i)f_\alpha,
    \quad 
    [e_\alpha,f_\alpha]=h_\alpha,
\end{align}
where $h_\alpha\in\mathfrak h$
denotes the coroot associated with
$\alpha$ (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:coroots}).
<!-- end mydef-18 -->
<!-- mydef-19: body_md -->
{Cartan Gram Matrix}{Cartan_Gram_Matrix}
Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and let
$\{h_1,\ldots,h_r\}$ be the generators of $\mathfrak h$ (see Def.~\ref{def:Chevalley_Basis}), with
$r=\mathrm{rank}(\mathfrak{g})$. 
Since the invariant bilinear form $\kappa$ is positive definite when restricted to the real span $\mathfrak{h}_{\mathbb R} = \mathrm{span}_{\mathbb R}\{h_1,\ldots,h_r\}$, the associated Cartan Gram matrix 
\begin{align}
    G\coloneqq (G_{ij})_{1\leqslant i,j\leqslant r},
\end{align}
with
\begin{align}\label{eq:Cartan_Gram_Matrix}
G_{ij}
\coloneqq
\kappa(h_i,h_j),
\end{align}
 is real, symmetric, and positive definite.
<!-- end mydef-19 -->
<!-- mydef-20: body_md -->
{Anti-Hermitian Basis}{Anti_Hermitian_Basis}
Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a complex semisimple Lie algebra with compact real form $\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R}$, and let $\{h_i,e_\alpha,f_\alpha\}$
be a Chevalley basis of $\mathfrak{g}$
(see Def.~\ref{def:Chevalley_Basis}).
The anti-Hermitian basis associated with this Chevalley basis is defined by
\begin{align}
    \{H_i, E_\alpha, F_\alpha
    \mid
    i=1,\dots,r,\,
    \alpha\in\Phi^+\},
\end{align}
where the Cartan generators $\{H_i\}_{i=1}^{r}$ are given by Eq.~\eqref{eq:orthogonalized_H_i}, and the generators of the root spaces are
\begin{align}
E_\alpha
&\coloneqq
-\mathrm{i}\sqrt{\frac{\langle \alpha,\alpha\rangle}{2}}(e_\alpha+f_\alpha),
\label{eq:anti_hermitian_root_generators_E}
\\
F_\alpha
&\coloneqq
-\sqrt{\frac{\langle \alpha,\alpha\rangle}{2}} (e_\alpha-f_\alpha)
.\label{eq:anti_hermitian_root_generators_F}
\end{align}
<!-- end mydef-20 -->
<!-- mylem-4: body_md -->
{Anti-Hermitian Property}{Anti_Hermitian}
The generators
$\{H_i,E_\alpha,F_\alpha\}$ (see Def.~\ref{def:Anti_Hermitian_Basis})
form an anti-Hermitian basis of the compact real form
$\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R}$.
Explicitly, each generator satisfies the condition
\begin{align}
    H_i^\dagger
    =-H_i, 
    \quad
    E_\alpha^\dagger
    =-E_\alpha,
    \quad
    F_\alpha^\dagger
    =-F_\alpha.
\end{align}
<!-- end mylem-4 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Using
\begin{align}
    h_i^\dagger=h_i,
    \quad
    e_\alpha^\dagger=f_\alpha,
    \quad
    f_\alpha^\dagger=e_\alpha,
\end{align}
together with the fact that $U_{ij}\in\mathbb R$, the anti-Hermiticity of the generators follows directly. 
For the Cartan generators $\{H_i\}_{i=1}^{r}$ (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:orthogonalized_H_i}),
\begin{align}
    H_i^\dagger
    &=
    \left(\sum_{j=1}^{r} -\mathrm{i}U_{ij}h_j\right)^\dagger
    =
    \sum_{j=1}^{r} \mathrm{i}U_{ij}h_j
    =
    -H_i,
\end{align}
Here $U\in\mathrm{GL}_r(\mathbb R)$ denotes the real invertible matrix introduced in Eq.~\eqref{eq:Cartan_orthonormalization_matrix}.
Similarly, for each positive root $\alpha\in\Phi^+$,
\begin{align}
   E_\alpha^\dagger
    &=
    \bigl(-\mathrm{i}\sqrt{\langle\alpha,\alpha\rangle/2}(e_\alpha+f_\alpha)\bigr)^\dagger
    =
    \mathrm{i}\sqrt{\langle\alpha,\alpha\rangle/2}(f_\alpha+e_\alpha)
    =
    -E_\alpha ,\\
    F_\alpha^\dagger
    &=
    \big(-\sqrt{\langle\alpha,\alpha\rangle/2}(e_\alpha-f_\alpha)\big)^\dagger
    =
    \sqrt{\langle\alpha,\alpha\rangle/2}(e_\alpha-f_\alpha)
    =
    -F_\alpha.
\end{align}
Thus all generators are anti-Hermitian, completing the proof.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- mythm-1: body_md -->
{Weight Space Decomposition}{Weight_Space_Decomposition}
Every finite-dimensional representation $V$ decomposes into weight spaces
\begin{align}
    V
    =
    \bigoplus_{\mu\in\mathfrak h^*}
    V_\mu,
\end{align}
where
\begin{align}
    V_\mu
    \coloneqq
    \{
    \psi\in V
    \mid
    \pi(h)\ket{\psi}
    =
    \mu(h)\ket{\psi},
    \ \forall\,h\in\mathfrak h
    \}
\end{align}
is the simultaneous eigenspace of the Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ with eigenvalue functional $\mu\in\mathfrak h^*$.
Whenever $V_\mu\neq\{0\}$, the corresponding functional $\mu$ is called a weight of the representation.
<!-- end mythm-1 -->
<!-- mydef-21: body_md -->
{Highest Weight Vector}{Highest_Weight_Vector}
A nonzero vector $\ket{\psi_{\Lambda}}\in V$ is called a highest weight vector of weight $\Lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$ if it satisfies the following conditions:
\begin{alignat}{2}
    \pi(h)\ket{\psi_{\Lambda}}
    &= \Lambda(h)\ket{\psi_{\Lambda}},
    &&\qquad \forall\,h\in\mathfrak h,
    \\
    \pi(e_\alpha)\ket{\psi_{\Lambda}}
    &= 0,
    &&\qquad \forall\,\alpha\in\Phi^+.
\end{alignat}
<!-- end mydef-21 -->
<!-- mylem-5: body_md -->
{Extremal Characterization of the Highest Weight}{Extremal_Characterization_Highest_Weight}
Let $V(\Lambda)$ be the finite-dimensional irreducible highest weight representation of $\mathfrak{g}$ associated with the positive root system $\Phi^+$, and let $\Lambda$ be its highest weight.
Then every weight $\mu\in V(\Lambda)$ satisfies
\begin{align}
\label{eq:norm_inequality}
    \langle\mu,\mu\rangle 
    \leqslant
    \langle\Lambda,\Lambda\rangle,
\end{align}
where $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ denotes the inner product on the real root space $E$ (see Def.~\ref{def:Inner_Product_Root_Space}).
Moreover, equality holds precisely for the extremal weights, namely those lying in the Weyl group orbit of $\Lambda$.
<!-- end mylem-5 -->
<!-- mydef-22: body_md -->
{Variance for Anti-Hermitian Operators}{Variance_Anti_Hermitian_Operators}
For an anti-Hermitian operator $X\in\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R}$, its variance in the quantum state $\psi$ is defined by 
\begin{align}\label{eq:non_hermitian_variance}
    \Delta_{\psi}^2(X)
    \coloneqq
    \langle X^\dagger X\rangle_{\psi}
    -
    \langle X^\dagger\rangle_{\psi}
    \langle X\rangle_{\psi}.
\end{align}
<!-- end mydef-22 -->
<!-- mylem-6: body_md -->
{Non-Negativity}{Non_Negativity}
The variance introduced in Def.~\ref{def:Variance_Anti_Hermitian_Operators} is non-negative for any anti-Hermitian operator $X\in\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R}$ and any quantum state $\psi$:
\begin{align}
    \Delta_{\psi}^2(X)\geqslant0.
\end{align}
<!-- end mylem-6 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
We begin the proof by rewriting the variance defined in Def.~\ref{def:Variance_Anti_Hermitian_Operators} as follows 
\begin{align}
    \Delta_{\psi}^2(X)
    &=
    \langle X^\dagger X\rangle_{\psi}-\langle X^\dagger\rangle_{\psi}\langle X\rangle_{\psi}\\
    &=
    \bra{\psi}\bigl(\pi(X)-\langle X\rangle_{\psi}\bigr)^\dagger\bigl(\pi(X)-\langle X\rangle_{\psi}\bigr)\ket{\psi}\\
    &=
    \left\|\bigl(\pi(X)-\langle X\rangle_{\psi}\bigr)\ket{\psi}\right\|^2\\
    &\geqslant0.
\end{align}
The variance $\Delta_{\psi}^2(X)$ is therefore non-negative, as claimed.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- mylem-7: body_md -->
{Variance Equivalence Under Hermitianization}{Variance_Equivalence_Under_Hermitianization}
For any anti-Hermitian generator $\pi(X)$, multiplication by $\mathrm{i}$ produces the corresponding Hermitian observable $\mathrm{i}\pi(X)$.
The generalized variance (see Def.~\ref{def:Variance_Anti_Hermitian_Operators}) of $\pi(X)$ therefore coincides exactly with the ordinary quantum variance of the Hermitian observable $\mathrm{i}\pi(X)$; namely
\begin{align}
    \Delta_{\psi}^2(X)=
    \Delta_{\psi}^2(\pi(X))=
    \Delta_{\psi}^2(\mathrm{i}\pi(X))=
    \Delta_{\psi}^2(\mathrm{i}X).
\end{align}
<!-- end mylem-7 -->
<!-- mydef-23: body_md -->
{Lie Algebraic Quantum Uncertainty}{Lie_Algebraic_Uncertainty_Relations}
Let $\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R}$ be a compact real semisimple Lie algebra (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:complexification}) equipped with an anti-Hermitian basis $\{H_i,E_\alpha,F_\alpha\}$ (see Def.~\ref{def:Anti_Hermitian_Basis}), and let $\ket{\psi}$ be a quantum state in a unitary representation space $V$ of $\pi:\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R}\to\mathfrak{gl}(V)$. 
We fix the normalization of the basis by requiring that, for any $Q_a, Q_b\in\{H_i,E_\alpha,F_\alpha\}$, $(Q_a,Q_b)=2\delta_{ab}$.
Here $(\cdot,\cdot)$ is the inner product defined in Def.~\ref{def:Inner_product_alg}.
The Lie algebra quantum uncertainty associated with $\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R}$ is defined as follows
\begin{align}
\label{eq:QUncertainty_Lie_Algebra}
    \Delta_{\psi}^2(\mathfrak{g}) \coloneqq \frac12\Biggl(\sum_{i=1}^r\Delta_{\psi}^2(H_i)
    +\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}
    \bigl(\Delta_{\psi}^2(E_\alpha)
    +\Delta_{\psi}^2(F_\alpha)\bigr)\Biggr).
\end{align}
Here, $r$ denotes the dimension of the Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, equivalently the rank of $\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R}$, i.e., $r=\dim_{\mathbb C}{\mathfrak h}=\mathrm{rank} \mathfrak{g}$, and $\Phi^+$ denotes a fixed choice of positive roots. 
The variances are not properties of the abstract Lie algebra alone. They are computed only after a representation $\pi$ has been chosen, and hence depend on the concrete action of the generators on the space $V$.
This formulation contains, as its simplest instance, $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb C)$, the complexification of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:Complexification_su_2}), where it recovers the conventional uncertainty relations of angular momentum.
When no ambiguity can arise, we will also write the uncertainty $\Delta_{\psi}^2(\mathfrak{g})$ as $\Delta_{\psi}^2(\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R})$, to emphasize its association with the compact real form;
for example, $\Delta_{\psi}^2(\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb C))=\Delta_{\psi}^2(\mathfrak{su}(2))$.
<!-- end mydef-23 -->
<!-- mydef-24: body_md -->
{Quadratic Casimir Element}{Quadratic_Casimir_Element}
The quadratic Casimir element $C_2$ associated with the chosen generators $\{X_a\}$ of $\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R}$ and the normalized invariant bilinear form $\kappa$ in Eq.~\eqref{eq:normal_Killing} is defined by
\begin{align}\label{eq:Quadratic_Casimir_Element}
    C_2\coloneqq \sum_a X_a X^a,
\end{align}
where $\{X^a\}$ denotes the dual basis determined by Eq.~\eqref{eq:Dual_Basis}.
<!-- end mydef-24 -->
<!-- mylem-8: body_md -->
{Basis Independence of the Quadratic Casimir Element}{Basis_Independence_Casimir_Element}
The construction of the quadratic Casimir element $C_2$ defined in Eq.~\eqref{eq:Quadratic_Casimir_Element} is independent of the choice of basis $\{X_a\}$ of $\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R}$.
<!-- end mylem-8 -->
<!-- mythm-2: body_md -->
{Explicit Form of the Quadratic Casimir Element}{Explicit_Form_Casimir_Element}
The quadratic Casimir element $C_2$ defined in Eq.~\eqref{eq:Quadratic_Casimir_Element}, using the normalized form $\kappa$ of Eq.~\eqref{eq:normal_Killing}, takes the form

\begin{align}\label{eq:Quadratic_Casimir_Element_Explicit}
    C_2
    =-\frac12 \Biggl( \sum_{i=1}^r H_i^2
    +\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi^+} \bigl(E_\alpha^2
    + F_\alpha^2 \bigr)\Biggr),
\end{align}
where $\{H_i,E_\alpha,F_\alpha\}$ denotes the anti-Hermitian basis of $\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R}$ (see Def.~\ref{def:Anti_Hermitian_Basis}).
<!-- end mythm-2 -->
<!-- mycor-1: body_md -->
{Quantum Uncertainty in Terms of the Casimir Element}{Quantum_Uncertainty_Casimir_Element}
The quantum uncertainty (see Def.~\ref{def:Lie_Algebraic_Uncertainty_Relations}) associated with the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R}$ can be equivalently expressed as
\begin{align}\label{eq:casimir_variance}
    \Delta_{\psi}^2(\mathfrak{g})
    =\langle C_2\rangle_{\psi}
    + \frac12\Biggl(\sum_{i=1}^r\langle H_i\rangle_{\psi}^2
    +\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi^+} \bigl(\langle E_\alpha\rangle_{\psi}^2
    +\langle F_\alpha\rangle_{\psi}^2
    \bigr)
    \Biggr),
\end{align}
where $C_2$ denotes the Casimir element defined in Eq.~\eqref{eq:Quadratic_Casimir_Element}, whose explicit form is given in Eq.~\eqref{eq:Quadratic_Casimir_Element_Explicit}.
<!-- end mycor-1 -->
<!-- mythm-3: body_md -->
{Alternative Form of the Quadratic Casimir Element}{Alternative_Form_Casimir_Element}
Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a complex semisimple Lie algebra of rank $r$, with Cartan
subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, positive root system $\Phi^+$, and normalized invariant form $\kappa$ (Eq.~\eqref{eq:normal_Killing}). 
For the Chevalley basis $\{h_i, e_{\alpha}, f_{\alpha}\}$ of Def.~\ref{def:Chevalley_Basis}, the quadratic Casimir element takes the form
\begin{align}
    C_2
    =
    \sum_{i=1}^r h_ih^i
    +
    \sum_{\alpha\in\Phi^+} \frac{
    \langle\alpha,\alpha\rangle}{2}
    \bigl(e_\alpha f_\alpha+f_\alpha e_\alpha\bigr),
\end{align}
where $\{h^1,\dots,h^r\}$ is the $\kappa$-dual basis of $\{h_1,\dots,h_r\}$.
<!-- end mythm-3 -->
<!-- mythm-4: body_md -->
{Value of the Quadratic Casimir Element}{Value_Casimir_Element}
Let $V(\Lambda)$ be an irreducible highest weight representation of a semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$, with highest weight $\Lambda$. 
The quadratic Casimir element $C_2$ (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:Quadratic_Casimir_Element}) acts on $V(\Lambda)$ by scalar multiplication; that is
\begin{align}
    C_2
    =
    \langle\Lambda,\Lambda+2\delta\rangle\1_{V(\Lambda)},
\end{align}
where $\delta=\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}\alpha/2$ is the Weyl vector (see Def.~\ref{def:Weyl_Vector}). 
Consequently, for any quantum state $\ket{\psi}\in V(\Lambda)$, the expectation value of $C_2$ is
\begin{align}
\label{eq:exp_Casimir}
    \langle C_2\rangle_{\psi}
    =
    \langle\Lambda,\Lambda+2\delta\rangle.
\end{align}
<!-- end mythm-4 -->
<!-- mylem-9: body_md -->
{Lie Algebraic Uncertainty Identity}{Lie_Algebraic_Uncertainty_Identity}
Let $V(\Lambda)$ be an irreducible highest weight representation (see Subsec.~\ref{subsec:Highest_Weight_Representations}) of Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$. 
Then every state $\ket{\psi}\in V(\Lambda)$ satisfies the Lie algebraic uncertainty relation
\begin{align}
\label{eq:decomp_chevalley1}
    \Delta^2_{\psi}(\mathfrak{g})
    = 
    \underbrace{\langle C_2\rangle_{\psi}}_{\text{State-Independent}}
    + 
    \underbrace{\frac12 \sum_{i=1}^r \langle H_i\rangle_{\psi}^2
    - \sum_{\alpha\in\Phi^+} \langle \alpha,\alpha\rangle\bigl| \langle e_\alpha\rangle_{\psi}\bigr|^2}_{\text{State-Dependent}},
\end{align}
where $C_2$ is the quadratic Casimir element (see Def.~\ref{def:Quadratic_Casimir_Element}).
<!-- end mylem-9 -->
<!-- mylem-10: body_md -->
{Lie Algebraic Uncertainty Identity in Weight Spaces}{Lie_Algebraic_Uncertainty_Identity_Weight}
Let $V_{\Lambda,\mu}$ be a weight space of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ (see Thm.~\ref{thm:Weight_Space_Decomposition}). 
The Lie algebraic quantum uncertainty of any state $\ket{\psi_{\mu}}\in V_{\Lambda,\mu}$ separates into a weight-independent Casimir contribution and weight-dependent Cartan terms determined by $\mu$,
\begin{align}
\label{eq:decomp_chevalley2}
    \Delta^2_{\psi_{\mu}}(\mathfrak{g})
    = 
    \underbrace{\langle C_2\rangle_{\psi_{\mu}}}_{\text{Weight-Independent}}
    + 
    \underbrace{\frac12 \sum_{i=1}^r \mu(H_i)^2}_{\text{Weight-Dependent}},
\end{align}
Here $C_2$ denotes the quadratic Casimir element of $\mathfrak{g}$, as defined in Def.~\ref{def:Quadratic_Casimir_Element}.
<!-- end mylem-10 -->
<!-- mythm-5: body_md -->
{Lie Algebraic Uncertainty Identity in Weight Spaces}{Lie_Algebraic_Uncertainty_Identity_Weight}
Let $V_{\Lambda,\mu}$ be a weight space of the irreducible highest weight representation $V(\Lambda)$ of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$, as in Thm.~\ref{thm:Weight_Space_Decomposition}.
Then, for any state $\ket{\psi_{\mu}}\in V_{\Lambda,\mu}$, the Lie algebraic quantum uncertainty reduces to a Casimir contribution and a weight dependent term determined by the inner product of $\mu$,
\begin{align}\label{eq:decomp_weight_final}
    \Delta_{\psi_{\mu}}^2(\mathfrak{g})
    = 
    \underbrace{\langle C_2\rangle_{\psi_\mu}}_{\text{Weight-Independent}}
    - 
    \underbrace{\langle\mu,\mu\rangle\, ,}_{\text{Weight-Dependent}}
\end{align}
where $C_2$ is the quadratic Casimir element of $\mathfrak{g}$, defined in Def.~\ref{def:Quadratic_Casimir_Element}.
<!-- end mythm-5 -->
<!-- mycor-2: body_md -->
{Lie Algebraic Uncertainty Bound in Weight Spaces}{Weight_Bound}
Let $V_{\Lambda, \mu}\subset V(\Lambda)$ be a weight space of an irreducible highest weight representation with highest weight $\Lambda$
(see Thm.~\ref{thm:Weight_Space_Decomposition}).
For every state $\ket{\psi_{\mu}}\in V_{\Lambda,\mu}$,
\begin{align}
    \Delta_{\psi_{\mu}}^2(\mathfrak{g})
    \geqslant
    \underbrace{2\langle\Lambda,\delta\rangle \, .}_{\text{Weight-Independent}}
\end{align}
Equality holds if and only if the weight $\mu$ lies in the Weyl group orbit of the highest weight $\Lambda$.
<!-- end mycor-2 -->
<!-- mydef-25: body_md -->
{Moment Element on $\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R}$}{Moment_Element}
Let $\ket{\psi}\in V(\Lambda)$ be a quantum state, and let $\{Q_a\}_{a}=\{H_i,E_\alpha,F_\alpha\}$ denote the anti-Hermitian generator basis (see Def.~\ref{def:Anti_Hermitian_Basis}) of the compact real Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R}$.
Using the real coefficients $m_a(\psi)$ defined in Eq.~\eqref{eq:m_a_psi}, we define the associated moment element by
\begin{align}
    M_{\psi} \coloneqq  \frac12 \sum_a m_a(\psi)\,Q_a \in \mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R} .
\end{align}
<!-- end mydef-25 -->
<!-- mylem-11: body_md -->
{Quantum Uncertainty in Terms of the Moment Element}{Quantum_Uncertainty_Moment_Element}
For the compact real Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R}$, the Lie algebraic quantum uncertainty of Def.~\ref{def:Lie_Algebraic_Uncertainty_Relations} admits the following equivalent expression
\begin{align}
\label{eq:variance_moment}
    \Delta_{\psi}^2(\mathfrak{g})
    = \langle\Lambda,\Lambda+2\delta\rangle
    - \|M_{\psi}\|^2 .
\end{align}
Here $M_{\psi}$ is the moment element associated with the state $\psi$ (see Def.~\ref{def:Moment_Element}), and $\delta$ denotes the Weyl vector (see Def.~\ref{def:Weyl_Vector}).
This identity holds for every quantum state $\ket{\psi}\in V(\Lambda)$.
<!-- end mylem-11 -->
<!-- mylem-12: body_md -->
{Moment-Norm Bound}{Moment_Norm_Bound}
Let $V(\Lambda)$ be a finite-dimensional highest weight representation of $\mathfrak{g}$, with highest weight $\Lambda$.
Then, for every state $\ket{\psi}\in V(\Lambda)$, the associated moment element $M_{\psi}$ (see Def.~\ref{def:Moment_Element}) satisfies
\begin{align}
\label{eq:moment_norm_bound}
    \|M_{\psi}\|^2
      \leqslant
    \langle\Lambda,\Lambda\rangle .
\end{align}
<!-- end mylem-12 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
For an arbitrary element
\begin{align}
    X=\sum_a x_a Q_a\in \mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R} ,
\end{align}
its inner product (see Def.~\ref{def:Inner_product_alg}) with the moment element $M_{\psi}$ is
\begin{align}
    (M_{\psi},X)
    &=\left(\frac12\sum_a m_a(\psi) Q_a,\sum_b x_b Q_b \right) \\
    &= \sum_a x_a m_a(\psi)\\
    &= \sum_a x_a\langle \mathrm{i} Q_a\rangle_\psi\\
    &=\langle \mathrm{i}X\rangle_{\psi} .
\end{align}
Thus, with respect to the inner product $(\cdot,\cdot)$ in Def.~\ref{def:Inner_product_alg}, $M_{\psi}$ represents the real linear functional
\begin{align}
     M_{\psi}: X\mapsto \langle \mathrm{i}X\rangle_\psi
\end{align}
on $\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R}$. 
This allows us to express the vector norm $\|M_{\psi}\|$ as the norm of the linear functional represented by $M_{\psi}$ as
(we still use the same symbol)
\begin{align}
\label{eq:moment_dual_norm}
    \|M_{\psi}\|
    \coloneqq
    \frac{1}{\sqrt2}
    \sup_{(X,X)=2}
    |\langle \mathrm{i}X\rangle_{\psi}| ,
\end{align}
where the supremum is over normalized anti-Hermitian operators $X\in\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R}$ with $(X,X)=2$.
Physically, $\sqrt{2}\|M_{\psi}\|$ represents the largest abolute expectation value attainable by the quantum state $\psi$ over all observables $\mathrm{i}X$ in the Lie algebra subject to $(X,X)=2$.

It remains to bound $|\langle \mathrm{i}X\rangle_\psi|$ for elements $X\in\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R}$ with $(X,X)=2$. 
Let $G$ be the connected, simply connected compact Lie group with Lie algebra $\mathfrak g_{\mathbb R}$, and let $\mathfrak t=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{H_i\}=-\mathrm{i}\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$ be its compact Cartan subalgebra. 
Every  $X\in \mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R}$ is conjugate under $G$ to some $A\in \mathfrak{t}$:  there exist $g\in G$ and $A\in \mathfrak{t}$ such that 
\begin{align}\label{eq:Conjugation}
    X=\mathrm{Ad}_g A=gAg^{-1} .
\end{align}
The adjoint invariance of the inner product $(\cdot,\cdot)$ ensures that the conjugation in Eq.~\eqref{eq:Conjugation} preserves the norm, namely
\begin{align}\label{eq:A_X_2}
    (A,A)=(X,X)=2 .
\end{align}
It therefore suffices to bound the expectation of normalized elements of $\mathfrak{t}=-\mathrm{i}\mathfrak{h}_{\mathbb R}$ uniformly over all states in $V(\Lambda)$.
  
In the representation $V(\Lambda)$, the adjoint conjugation $X=\mathrm{Ad}_g A$ is implemented by the corresponding unitary action of the compact group:
\begin{align}\label{eq:pi_A_X_commutative}
    \pi(X)
    =
    U_g\,\pi(A)\,U_g^\dagger .
\end{align}
where $U_g$ denotes the unitary operator representing $g$ on $V(\Lambda)$. 
This equivalence (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:pi_A_X_commutative}) is captured by the following commutative diagram:
\begin{equation}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=huge, column sep=huge]
V(\Lambda) \arrow[r, "\pi(A)"] \arrow[d, "U_g"'] & 
V(\Lambda) \arrow[d, "U_g"] \\
V(\Lambda) \arrow[r, "\pi(X)"'] & 
V(\Lambda)
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}
Hence $\pi(X)$ and $\pi(A)$ are unitarily equivalent and, in particular, have the same spectrum.
Equivalently, by introducing the transformed state
\begin{align}
    \ket{\phi}
    \coloneqq
    U_g^\dagger \ket{\psi},
\end{align}
we obtain
\begin{align}
    \langle \mathrm{i}X\rangle_\psi
    =
    \bra{\psi}\mathrm{i}\pi(X)\ket{\psi}
    =
    \bra{\phi}\mathrm{i}\pi(A)\ket{\phi}
    =
    \langle \mathrm{i}A\rangle_\phi .
\end{align}
We can therefore use the Cartan spectrum to bound the expectation in the transformed state $\phi$. Since $A\in \mathfrak{t}$, it acts on $V_{\Lambda,\mu}$ by $\mu(A)$, and $\mathrm{i}A$ has eigenvalue $\mathrm{i}\mu(A)$. 
The spectral bound on expectation values gives
\begin{align}
\label{eq:spectral_bound}
    |\langle \mathrm{i}X\rangle_\psi|
    =
    |\langle \mathrm{i}A\rangle_\phi|
    \leqslant
    \max_{\mu\in\Omega(\Lambda)}
    |\mu(A)| .
\end{align}
Write
\begin{align}
A=\sum_{i=1}^r a_iH_i
\end{align}
in a Cartan basis normalized as $(H_i,H_j)=2\delta_{ij}$.
The constraint $(A,A)=2$ (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:A_X_2}) is then equivalent to
\begin{align}
    \sum_{i=1}^r a_i^2=1.
\end{align}
Therefore, for any weight $\mu$,
\begin{align} \label{eq:maximal_mu}
    |\mu(A)|^2
    =
    \left| \sum_{i=1}^r a_i\mu(H_i)\right|^2
    \leqslant
    \sum_{i=1}^r |\mu(H_i)|^2 .
\end{align}
The last step is the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.
The right-hand side of Eq.~\eqref{eq:maximal_mu} is twice the squared weight norm.   
For the anti-Hermitian Cartan generators,
\begin{align}
    \frac12\sum_{i=1}^r |\mu(H_i)|^2 
    &=
    \frac12\sum_{i=1}^r \overline{\mu(H_i)}\,\mu(H_i) \\
    &=
    \frac12 \sum_{i=1}^r \mu(H_i^\dagger)\mu(H_i) \\
    &=
    -\frac12\sum_{i=1}^r \mu(H_i)\mu(H_i) \\
    &=
    \sum_{i=1}^r\mu(H_i)\mu(H^i) \\
    &=
    \langle\mu,\mu\rangle .
\end{align}
Hence
\begin{align}
    |\mu(A)|
      \leqslant 
    \sqrt{2\langle\mu,\mu\rangle}\, .
\end{align}
For an irreducible highest weight representation $V(\Lambda)$, every weight $\mu$ satisfies $\langle\mu,\mu\rangle\leqslant\langle\Lambda,\Lambda\rangle$.
Combining these gives the expectation value bound
\begin{align}
    |\langle \mathrm{i}X\rangle_\psi| 
    =
    |\langle \mathrm{i}A\rangle_\phi|
      \leqslant 
    \sqrt{2\langle\Lambda,\Lambda\rangle} .
\end{align}
Taking the supremum over all normalized Lie algebra elements $X$ in Eq.~\eqref{eq:moment_dual_norm} therefore yields
\begin{align}
    \|M_\psi\|
      \leqslant 
    \sqrt{\langle\Lambda,\Lambda\rangle} \,,
\end{align}
or equivalently,
\begin{align}
    \|M_\psi\|^2
      \leqslant 
    \langle\Lambda,\Lambda\rangle\, .
\end{align}
This establishes the desired bound on the moment element $M_{\psi}$ and completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- mythm-6: body_md -->
{Lie Algebraic Uncertainty Relations}{Lie_Algebraic_Uncertainty_Relations}
Let $V(\Lambda)$ be an irreducible highest weight representation of the compact semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R}$.
The Lie algebraic uncertainty is bounded from below across the entire representation space: 
for every quantum state $\ket{\psi}\in V(\Lambda)$ 
\begin{align}
\label{eq:general_uncertainty_bound}
    \Delta_\psi^2(\mathfrak{g})
     \geqslant 2\langle\Lambda,\delta\rangle \,,
\end{align}
where $\delta$ denotes the Weyl vector (see Def.~\ref{def:Weyl_Vector}), defined as half the sum of all positive roots.
<!-- end mythm-6 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Substituting the moment-norm estimate of Eq.~\eqref{eq:moment_norm_bound} into the uncertainty identity Eq.~\eqref{eq:variance_moment}, one finds
\begin{align}
    \Delta_\psi^2(\mathfrak{g})
    = 
    \langle\Lambda,\Lambda+2\delta\rangle
    - \|M_{\psi}\|^2 \geqslant
    \langle\Lambda,\Lambda+2\delta\rangle
    - \langle\Lambda,\Lambda\rangle
    =
    2\langle\Lambda,\delta\rangle .
\end{align}
The bound is independent of $\psi$, and therefore holds uniformly over the full representation space $V(\Lambda)$, completing the proof.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- mycor-3: body_md -->
{Uncertainty Identity for Spin-$j$ Uncertainty at Fixed Magnetic Quantum Number}{Conservation_Law_Magnetic_Quantum_Number}
In the spin-$j$ representation of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$, the total quantum uncertainty of a weight state $|\psi_{\mu_m}\rangle\in V_{j,m}$ is conserved at fixed magnetic quantum number $m$, and Eq.~\eqref{eq:decomp_weight_final} reduces to 
\begin{align}
    \Delta^2_{\psi_{\mu_m}}(\mathfrak{su}(2))
    =
    \underbrace{2j(j+1)}_{\text{Highest-Weight-Dependent}}
    -
    \underbrace{2m^2}_{\text{Weight-Dependent}},
\end{align}
Equivalently, in terms of the physical angular momentum observables, one obtains 
\begin{align}\label{eq:magnetic_uncertainty}
     \Delta_{\psi_{\mu_m}}^2(J_x) + \Delta_{\psi_{\mu_m}}^2(J_y) + \Delta_{\psi_{\mu_m}}^2(J_z)
    =
    \frac{1}{2}\Delta^2_{\psi_{\mu_m}}(\mathfrak{su}(2))
    =
    \underbrace{j(j+1)}_{\text{Highest-Weight-Dependent}}
    -
    \underbrace{m^2}_{\text{Weight-Dependent}}.
\end{align}
Thus, within each fixed weight sector, the total angular momentum uncertainty is fixed by the magnetic quantum number $m$. 
It attains its minimum at the extremal weights $m=\pm j$.
<!-- end mycor-3 -->
<!-- mycor-4: body_md -->
{Angular Momentum Uncertainty Relation}{Angular_Momentum_Uncertainty_Relation}
In the spin-$j$ representation of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$, Eq.~\eqref{eq:variance_moment} gives the Lie algebraic uncertainty of a quantum state $\ket{\psi}\in V_{j}$ as
\begin{align}
    \Delta^2_{\psi}(\mathfrak{su}(2))
    \geqslant
    2j\,,
\end{align}
Equivalently, when expressed in terms of the physical angular momentum, this becomes 
\begin{align}\label{eq:angular_momentum_uncertainty}
     \Delta_{\psi}^2(J_x) + 
     \Delta_{\psi}^2(J_y) + 
     \Delta_{\psi}^2(J_z)
    =
    \frac{1}{2}\Delta^2_{\psi}(\mathfrak{su}(2))
    \geqslant
    j\,.
\end{align}
Thus, the optimal lower bound on the total angular momentum uncertainty is completely determined by the spin quantum number $j$.
<!-- end mycor-4 -->
<!-- mycor-5: body_md -->
{Uncertainty Identity for $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ Uncertainty in Weight Spaces}{su3_Weight_Space_Uncertainty}
Let $V(\Lambda)$ be an irreducible $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ representation with highest weight $\Lambda$, and let $\mu$ denote a weight. 
With the expansions of $\Lambda$ and $\mu$ in the fundamental weight basis specified in Eqs.~\eqref{eq:su_3_Highest_Weight} and~\eqref{eq:su_3_Weight}, the corresponding Lie algebraic uncertainty relation on $V_{\Lambda, \mu}$ space reads
\begin{align}
\label{eq:su3_weight_conservation}
    \Delta_{\psi_\mu}^2(\mathfrak{su}(3))
    =
    \underbrace{
    \frac{2}{3}
    \left(\lambda_1^2+\lambda_1\lambda_2+\lambda_2^2 \right)
     +
    2(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)
    }_{\text{Highest-Weight-Dependent}}
    -
    \underbrace{
    \frac{2}{3} \left(m_1^2+m_1m_2+m_2^2\right)
    }_{\text{Weight-Dependent}}.
\end{align}
Thus, for a fixed highest weight $\Lambda$, the Lie algebraic uncertainty in each $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ weight sector $V_{\Lambda, \mu}$ is specified entirely by the two weight labels $m_1$ and $m_2$ (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:su_3_Weight}).
<!-- end mycor-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
In the case of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$, the associated root system is of type $A_2$, with the corresponding Dynkin diagram shown below. 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:DynkinAtwonumber}
    \raisebox{-2.8ex}{\includegraphics[scale=1]{DK_A_2_No.pdf}}\, .
\end{equation}
Denote the two simple roots by $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$, as shown in Eq.~\eqref{eq:DynkinAtwonumber}, and choose the normalization 
\begin{align}\label{eq:}
    \langle\alpha_1,\alpha_1\rangle
    =
    \langle\alpha_2,\alpha_2\rangle
    =
    2.
\end{align}
With this convention, the inner product between distinct simple roots is given by
\begin{align}
    \langle\alpha_1,\alpha_2\rangle
    =
    -1.
\end{align}

The fundamental weights (see Def.~\ref{def:Fundamental_Weights}) are defined as the basis dual to the simple coroots. 
For $\mathfrak{su}(3)$, they are denoted by $\omega_1$, $\omega_2$, and satisfy the duality relations
\begin{align}
    \frac{
    2\langle\omega_i,\alpha_j\rangle
    }{
    \langle\alpha_j,\alpha_j\rangle
    }
    =
    \delta_{ij},
    \quad
    i,j\in\{1,2\}.
\end{align}
Under the normalization
\begin{align}
    \langle\alpha_j,\alpha_j\rangle=2,
\end{align}
the defining duality relations reduce to
\begin{align}
    \langle\omega_i,\alpha_j\rangle
    =
    \delta_{ij}.
\end{align}
To express the simple roots in the basis of fundamental weights, write
\begin{align}
    \alpha_1
    =
    a_{11}\omega_1+a_{12}\omega_2.
\end{align}
Pairing both sides with $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$ then gives
\begin{align}
    a_{11}
    &=
    \langle\alpha_1,\alpha_1\rangle
    =
    2,\\
    a_{12}
    &=
    \langle\alpha_1,\alpha_2\rangle
    =
    -1.
\end{align}
Thus the first simple root $\alpha_1$ (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:DynkinAtwonumber}) has the expansion
\begin{align}
\label{eq:alpha1}
\alpha_1=2\omega_1-\omega_2,
\end{align}
in the basis of fundamental weights $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$.

Likewise, expanding the second simple root $\alpha_2$ (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:DynkinAtwonumber}) as
\begin{align}
    \alpha_2
    =
    a_{21}\omega_1+a_{22}\omega_2,
\end{align}
and pairing with the two simple roots gives
\begin{align}
    a_{21}
    &=
    \langle\alpha_2,\alpha_1\rangle
    =-1,
    \\
    a_{22}
    &=
    \langle\alpha_2,\alpha_2\rangle
    =2.
\end{align}
Thus the second simple root $\alpha_2$ (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:DynkinAtwonumber}) has the expansion
\begin{align}
\label{eq:alpha2}
\alpha_2=-\omega_1+2\omega_2.
\end{align}

For $\mathfrak{su}(3)$, the positive roots are
\begin{align}
    \Phi^+
    =
    \{
    \alpha_1,
    \alpha_2,
    \alpha_1+\alpha_2
    \}.
\end{align}
The Weyl vector $\delta$ (see Def.~\ref{def:Weyl_Vector}) is therefore given by the half-sum of positive roots,
\begin{align}
    \delta
    =
    \frac12
    \sum_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}\alpha
    =
    \frac12
    \left(
    \alpha_1+\alpha_2+\left(\alpha_1+\alpha_2\right)
    \right)
    =
    \alpha_1+\alpha_2.
\end{align}
Using the expansions of the simple roots in the fundamental weights (see Eqs.~\eqref{eq:alpha1} and~\eqref{eq:alpha2}),
\begin{align}
\label{eq:alpha3}
    \alpha_1+\alpha_2
    =
    (2\omega_1-\omega_2)+(-\omega_1+2\omega_2)
    =
    \omega_1+\omega_2.
\end{align}
Hence the Weyl vector $\delta$ takes the simple form
\begin{align}
    \delta
    =
    \omega_1+\omega_2.
\end{align}

It remains to evaluate the inner products between the fundamental weights. 
The relations in Eqs.~\eqref{eq:alpha1} and \eqref{eq:alpha2} may be inverted to express the fundamental weights in the simple root basis:
\begin{align}
    \omega_1
    &=
    \frac23\alpha_1+\frac13\alpha_2,
    \\
    \omega_2
    &=
    \frac13\alpha_1+\frac23\alpha_2.
\end{align}
Using the root inner products, one obtains
\begin{align}
    \langle\omega_1,\omega_1\rangle
    =
    \langle\omega_2,\omega_2\rangle
    =
    \frac23,
\end{align}
and
\begin{align}
    \langle\omega_1,\omega_2\rangle
    =
    \frac13.
\end{align}

With these ingredients in place, the uncertainty identity in Thm.~\ref{thm:Lie_Algebraic_Uncertainty_Identity_Weight} can now be evaluated explicitly. 
The relevant quantity is $\langle C_2\rangle_{\psi_\mu}-\langle\mu,\mu\rangle$ (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:decomp_weight_final}).
The first term is fixed by the quadratic Casimir element $C_2$ of $\mathfrak{g}$. Here $\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{sl}(3,\mathbb C)$ with compact real form $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ (see Def.~\ref{def:Quadratic_Casimir_Element}). 
Let the highest weight $\Lambda$ of the irreducible representation be
\begin{align}
    \Lambda
    =
    \lambda_1\omega_1+\lambda_2\omega_2.
\end{align}
Then the quadratic Casimir element $C_2$ acts on $V(\Lambda)$ as multiplication by the scalar
\begin{align}
\label{eq:su3_casimir_value}
    \langle C_2\rangle\bigg|_{V(\Lambda)}
    =
    \langle\Lambda,\Lambda\rangle
    +
    2\langle\Lambda,\delta\rangle
    =
    \frac23
    \left(
    \lambda_1^2+\lambda_1\lambda_2+\lambda_2^2
    \right)
    +
    2(\lambda_1+\lambda_2).
\end{align}
Similarly, for a weight
\begin{align}
    \mu
    =
    m_1\omega_1+m_2\omega_2,
\end{align}
the norm is
\begin{align}
\label{eq:su3_weight_norm_explicit}
    \langle\mu,\mu\rangle
    =
    \frac23
    \left(
    m_1^2+m_1m_2+m_2^2
    \right).
\end{align}
Substituting Eqs.~\eqref{eq:su3_casimir_value}
and~\eqref{eq:su3_weight_norm_explicit} into Thm.~\ref{thm:Lie_Algebraic_Uncertainty_Identity_Weight} yields Eq.~\eqref{eq:su3_weight_conservation}, completing the proof.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- mycor-6: body_md -->
{Uncertainty Identity in the Defining Representation of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$}{LAU_Conservation_def_su3}
For the defining representation of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$, whose weights $\mu_1$, $\mu_2$, $\mu_3$ are given in Eq.~\eqref{eq:WeightAtwoDef}, the Lie algebraic uncertainty relation restricted to each weight space $V_{\Lambda, \mu_i}$ takes the form
\begin{align}
\label{eq:LAU_Conservation_def_su3}
    \Delta_{\psi_{\mu_1}}^2(\mathfrak{su}(3))
    =
    \Delta_{\psi_{\mu_2}}^2(\mathfrak{su}(3))
    =
    \Delta_{\psi_{\mu_3}}^2(\mathfrak{su}(3))
    =
    2.
\end{align}
Here, the Lie algebraic uncertainty is conserved across the full weight basis state of the defining representation; 
it is independent of the weight label $i$.
<!-- end mycor-6 -->
<!-- mycor-7: body_md -->
{Lie Algebraic Uncertainty in the Defining Representation of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$}{LAU_def_su3}
Consider the defining representation $V(\Lambda)$ of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$, whose highest weight is $\Lambda=\omega_1$.
For $\mathfrak{su}(3)$, the Weyl vector is $\delta=\omega_1+\omega_2$.
Then the Lie algebraic uncertainty is bounded from below over the entire representation space $V(\omega_1)$. 
Namely, for every normalized quantum state $\ket{\psi}\in V(\omega_1)$,
\begin{align}
\label{eq:LAU_def_su3}
    \Delta_{\psi}^2(\mathfrak{su}(3))
    \geqslant
    2.
\end{align}
<!-- end mycor-7 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
In this case, the optimal lower bound takes the form
\begin{align}
    2\langle\Lambda,\delta\rangle
    &=
    2\langle\omega_1,\omega_1+\omega_2\rangle\\
    &=
    2\left(\langle\omega_1,\omega_1\rangle+\langle\omega_1,\omega_2\rangle\right)\\
    &=
    2\left(\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{3}\right)\\
    &=
    2.
\end{align}
This establishes the desired result.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- mycor-8: body_md -->
{Uncertainty Identity in the Adjoint Representation of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ ($\mu\neq0$)}{LAU_Conservation_adj_su3_n0}
Consider the adjoint representation $V(\omega_1+\omega_2)$ of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$, whose non-zero weights are the six roots $\mu\in\Phi=\{\pm\alpha_1, \pm\alpha_2, \pm(\alpha_1+\alpha_2)\}$. 
Then, for every non-zero weight sector $V_{\omega_1+\omega_2,\mu}$ with $\mu\neq0$, the Lie algebraic uncertainty takes the constant value
\begin{align}
    \Delta_{\psi_\mu}^2(\mathfrak{su}(3))=4.
\end{align}
Hence, the Lie algebraic uncertainty is conserved across all non-zero weight sectors of the adjoint representation; 
it is independent of the choice of weight $\mu\in\Phi$.
<!-- end mycor-8 -->
<!-- mycor-9: body_md -->
{Uncertainty Identity in the Adjoint Representation of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ ($\mu=0$)}{LAU_Conservation_adj_su3_0}
Consider the adjoint representation $V(\omega_1+\omega_2)$ of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$.
Its zero-weight space is the Cartan subalgebra, i.e., $V_{\omega_1+\omega_2,0}=\mathfrak h$.
Then, for every state $\psi_0\in\mathfrak h$, the Lie algebraic uncertainty takes the value
\begin{align}
    \Delta_{\psi_0}^2(\mathfrak{su}(3))=6.
\end{align}
<!-- end mycor-9 -->
<!-- mycor-10: body_md -->
{Lie Algebraic Uncertainty in the Adjoint Representation of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$}{LAU_adj_su3}
Let $V(\Lambda)$ be the adjoint representation of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$, with highest weight $\Lambda=\omega_1+\omega_2$ and Weyl vector $\delta=\omega_1+\omega_2$.
The Lie algebraic uncertainty is bounded from below on the entire representation space $V(\omega_1+\omega_2)$. 
That is, for every state $\ket{\psi}\in V(\omega_1+\omega_2)$
\begin{align}
\label{eq:LAU_adj_su3}
    \Delta_{\psi}^2(\mathfrak{su}(3))
    \geqslant
    4.
\end{align}
<!-- end mycor-10 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
For the adjoint representation, the optimal lower bound is obtained as
\begin{align}
    2\langle\Lambda,\delta\rangle
    &=
    2\langle\omega_1+\omega_2,\omega_1+\omega_2\rangle \\
    &=
    2\Bigl(
        \langle\omega_1,\omega_1\rangle
        +
        \langle\omega_1,\omega_2\rangle
        +
        \langle\omega_2,\omega_1\rangle
        +
        \langle\omega_2,\omega_2\rangle
    \Bigr) \\
    &=
    2\left(
        \frac{2}{3}
        +
        \frac{1}{3}
        +
        \frac{1}{3}
        +
        \frac{2}{3}
    \right) \\
    &=
    4.
\end{align}
Hence the desired state-independent lower bound follows.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- mydef-26: body_md -->
{Covariance Matrix}{Covariance_Matrix}
Let $\mathbf X\coloneqq\{X_i\}_{i}$ be a family of operators on space $V$, not necessarily Hermitian. 
For a normalized state $\ket{\psi}$, their covariance is
\begin{align}\label{eq:general_nonhermitian_covariance_definition}
    \mathrm{Cov}_\psi(X_i,X_j)
    \coloneqq
    \langle X_i^\dagger X_j\rangle_\psi
    -\langle X_i^\dagger\rangle_\psi\langle X_j\rangle_\psi,
\end{align}
with the corresponding covariance matrix
\begin{align}\label{eq:general_nonhermitian_covariance_matrix}
    \mathrm{Cov}_\psi(\mathbf X)
    \coloneqq
    \left(\mathrm{Cov}_\psi(X_i,X_j)\right)_{i,j}.
\end{align}
<!-- end mydef-26 -->
<!-- mydef-27: body_md -->
{Gram Matrix}{Gram_Matrix_Generator_Basis}
For a family of operators $\mathbf X\coloneqq\{X_i\}_{i}$ in $\mathfrak{g}$, we define the associated Gram matrix $\mathrm{G}(\mathbf X)$ by
\begin{align}\label{eq:Gram_matirx}
    \mathrm{G}(\mathbf X)
    \coloneqq
    \left((X_i,X_j)_{\mathfrak{g}}\right)_{i, j}.
\end{align}
<!-- end mydef-27 -->
<!-- mydef-28: body_md -->
{Generalized Lie Algebraic Quantum Uncertainty}{Generalized_Lie_Algebraic_Uncertainty_Relations}
Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a Lie algebra with basis $\mathbf X$. We define the corresponding quantum uncertainty by
\begin{align}\label{eq:GUR_Lie}
    \Delta_\psi^2(\mathfrak{g})
    \coloneqq\Tr[\mathrm{G}(\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathrm{Cov}_\psi(\mathbf X)].
\end{align}
<!-- end mydef-28 -->
<!-- mythm-7: body_md -->
{Basis Independence of Generalized Lie Algebraic Quantum Uncertainty}{Basis_Independence_Orthogonal_Representation}
The quantum uncertainty $\Delta_\psi^2(\mathfrak{g})$ defined in Eq.~\eqref{eq:GUR_Lie} is independent of the choice of basis $\mathbf X$ of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$.
<!-- end mythm-7 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
The inner product and covariance are both sesquilinear, with conjugate linearity in the first argument. 
Thus, under an arbitrary change of basis $\mathbf Y=M\mathbf X$, where $M\in\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb C)$, we have
\begin{align}\label{eq:b5_covariance_basis_change}
    \mathrm{G}(\mathbf Y)&=\overline M \mathrm{G}(\mathbf X)M^{\mathbf{T}},
\end{align}
and
\begin{align}
    \mathrm{Cov}_\psi(\mathbf Y)&=\overline M\mathrm{Cov}_\psi(\mathbf X)M^{\mathbf{T}},
\end{align}
with $\overline M$ denoting entrywise complex conjugation. 
This implies
\begin{align}
    \mathrm{G}(\mathbf Y)^{-1}\mathrm{Cov}_\psi(\mathbf Y)
    =(M^{\mathbf{T}})^{-1}
    \mathrm{G}(\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathrm{Cov}_\psi(\mathbf X)M^{\mathbf{T}},
\end{align}
which leads to the same trace:
\begin{align}\label{eq:intrinsic_uncertainty_basis_independence}
    \Tr\!\left[\mathrm{G}(\mathbf Y)^{-1}\mathrm{Cov}_\psi(\mathbf Y)\right]
    =\Tr\!\left[\mathrm{G}(\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathrm{Cov}_\psi(\mathbf X)\right].
\end{align}
Hence $\Delta_\psi^2(\mathfrak{g})$ is independent of the chosen basis.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- mycor-11: body_md -->
{Generalized Lie Algebraic Quantum Uncertainty in the Chevalley Basis}{GUR_Chevalley}
In the Chevalley basis $\mathbf X_{\mathrm{Ch}}$ (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:GUR_Chevalley}), the quantum uncertainty $\Delta_\psi^2(\mathfrak{g})$ defined in Eq.~\eqref{eq:GUR_Lie} is given by
\begin{align}\label{eq:chevalley_uncertainty_explicit}
    \Delta_\psi^2(\mathfrak{g})
    =
    \sum_{i,j=1}^{r}(\mathrm{G}_{\mathfrak h}^{-1})_{ij}\mathrm{Cov}_\psi(h_i,h_j)
    +\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}\frac{\langle\alpha,\alpha\rangle}{2}
    \left(\Delta_\psi^2(e_\alpha)+\Delta_\psi^2(f_\alpha)\right).
\end{align}
<!-- end mycor-11 -->
<!-- mycor-12: body_md -->
{Generalized Lie Algebraic Quantum Uncertainty in the Anti-Hermitian Basis}{GUR_anti_Hermitian}
In the observable basis $\mathbf X_{\mathrm{aH}}$ specified in Eq.~\eqref{eq:GUR_anti_Hermitian}, the quantum uncertainty of Eq.~\eqref{eq:GUR_Lie} can be expressed as
\begin{align}\label{eq:anti_hermitian_uncertainty}
    \Delta_\psi^2(\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R})
    =\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Delta_\psi^2(H_i)
    +\frac12\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}
    \left(\Delta_\psi^2(E_\alpha)+\Delta_\psi^2(F_\alpha)\right).
\end{align}
<!-- end mycor-12 -->
<!-- mycor-13: body_md -->
{Generalized Lie Algebraic Quantum Uncertainty in the Observable Basis}{GUR_observable}
In the observable basis $\mathbf X_{\mathrm{ob}}$ defined in Eq.~\eqref{eq:GUR_observable}, the quantum uncertainty of Eq.~\eqref{eq:GUR_Lie} reduces to
\begin{align}\label{eq:observable_uncertainty}
    \Delta_\psi^2(i\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R})
    =
    \frac12\sum_{i=1}^{r}
    \Delta_\psi^2(\mathrm{i}H_i)
    +\frac12\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}
    \left(
    \Delta_\psi^2(\mathrm{i}E_\alpha)+
    \Delta_\psi^2(\mathrm{i}F_\alpha)\right).
\end{align}
<!-- end mycor-13 -->
<!-- mycor-14: body_md -->
{Equivalence of Uncertainty in Chevalley, Anti-Hermitian and Observable Bases}{Equivalence_Basis_Representations}
For a Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ equipped with an inner product $(\cdot,\cdot)_{\mathfrak{g}}$, the quantum uncertainty of a state $\psi$, defined in Eq.~\eqref{eq:inner_product_g}, admits equivalent expressions in the Chevalley, anti-Hermitian and observable bases:
\begin{align}\label{eq:three_formulations_equivalence}
        \Delta_\psi^2(\mathfrak{g})=\Delta_\psi^2(\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R})=\Delta_\psi^2(\mathrm{i}\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R}).
    \end{align}
<!-- end mycor-14 -->
<!-- mydef-29: body_md -->
{Fundamental Weights}{Fundamental_Weights}
For the simple roots $\Pi=\{\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r\}$ (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:simple_roots_set}), the fundamental weights $\Omega\coloneqq\{\omega_i\}_{i=1}^r$ are the basis of $\mathfrak{h}^*$ dual to the simple coroots. They satisfy
\begin{align}
\label{eq:fundamental_weights}
   \omega_i(h_{\alpha_j})
   =
   \frac{2\langle \omega_i,\alpha_j\rangle}
        {\langle \alpha_j,\alpha_j\rangle}
   =
   \delta_{ij},
   \quad 1\leqslant i,j\leqslant r,
\end{align}
where $h_{\alpha_j}$ is the coroot associated with the simple root $\alpha_j\in\Pi$.
<!-- end mydef-29 -->
<!-- mydef-30: body_md -->
{Dynkin Coefficients}{Dynkin_Coefficients}
Consider a finite-dimensional irreducible highest weight representation $V(\Lambda)$ of a complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$, with highest weight $\Lambda$. 
Once a system of simple roots $\Pi=\{\alpha_i\}_{i=1}^r$ (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:simple_roots_set}) has been fixed, the associated fundamental weights $\Omega=\{\omega_i\}_{i=1}^r$ form the basis dual to the simple coroots $\{h_{\alpha_i}\}_{i=1}^r$, as in Eq.~\eqref{eq:fundamental_weights}. 
They therefore provide the coordinates for highest weights. 
In this basis, $\Lambda$ admits the expansion
\begin{align}
\label{eq:highest_weight_expansion}
    \Lambda
    =\sum_{i=1}^r
    \lambda_i\omega_i,
\end{align}
The coefficients $\{\lambda_i\}_{i=1}^{r}$ are non-negative integers and are called the Dynkin coefficients of the representation $V(\Lambda)$, and they are given by
\begin{align}
\label{eq:dynkin_coefficients}
    \lambda_i
    =\Lambda(h_{\alpha_i})
    =\frac{2\langle\Lambda,\alpha_i\rangle}{\langle\alpha_i,\alpha_i\rangle }.
\end{align}
<!-- end mydef-30 -->
<!-- mydef-31: body_md -->
{Cartan Matrix}{Cartan_Matrix}
A choice of simple roots $\Pi=\{\alpha_i\}_{i=1}^r$ (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:simple_roots_set}) determines the corresponding simple coroots $\{h_{\alpha_j}\}_{j=1}^r$. 
The Cartan matrix is the matrix $C=(C_{ij})_{1\leqslant i,j\leqslant r}$ defined by
\begin{align}
    C\coloneqq(C_{ij})_{1\leqslant i,j\leqslant r},
\end{align}
with the coefficients
\begin{align}
\label{eq:Cartan_matrix}
    C_{ij} 
    \coloneqq
    \alpha_i(h_{\alpha_j})
    =
    \frac{2\langle\alpha_i,\alpha_j\rangle}{\langle\alpha_j,\alpha_j\rangle}.
\end{align}
In this convention, the $j$-th column of $C$ gives the evaluations of all simple roots on the simple coroot $h_{\alpha_j}$.
<!-- end mydef-31 -->
<!-- mythm-8: body_md -->
{Explicit Bounds for Lie Algebraic Uncertainty}{Explicit_Uncertainty_Bound}
Let $V(\Lambda)$ be an irreducible highest weight representation (see Subsec.~\ref{subsec:Highest_Weight_Representations}) of a complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ of rank $r$, with compact real form $\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R}$. 
Write the highest weight in the fundamental weight basis as $\Lambda=\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i\omega_i$ (see Def.~\ref{def:Fundamental_Weights}), where $\lambda_i\in\mathbb Z_{\geqslant 0}$ are the Dynkin coefficients (see Def.~\ref{def:Dynkin_Coefficients}) of the representation. 
Let $C$ be the Cartan matrix (see Def.~\ref{def:Cartan_Matrix}) of the  simple roots $\Pi=\{\alpha_i\}_{i=1}^r$ (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:simple_roots_set}), and let $C^{-1}$ denote its inverse. 
Then, for every quantum state $\ket{\psi}\in V(\Lambda)$, the Lie algebraic uncertainty satisfies
\begin{align}
\label{eq:final_bound}
    \Delta^2_{\psi}(\mathfrak{g})
    \geqslant \sum_{i,j=1}^r 
    \lambda_i C^{-1}_{ij} \langle\alpha_j,\alpha_j\rangle.
\end{align}
The bound is optimal and is attained by a highest-weight state (see Def.~\ref{def:Highest_Weight_Vector}) and its compact-group orbit.
Here $C^{-1}_{ij}$ denotes the $(i,j)$-entry of inverse Cartan matrix $C^{-1}$.
<!-- end mythm-8 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
A structural identity now becomes useful.
The Weyl vector (see Def.~\ref{def:Weyl_Vector}) has an especially simple form in the fundamental-weight basis: 
it is the sum of all fundamental weights.
\begin{align}
\label{eq:delta_sum}
    \delta
    =\sum_{i=1}^r \omega_i.
\end{align}
To see this, recall that the Weyl vector satisfies
\begin{align}
    \delta(h_{\alpha_j})
    =1,
\end{align}
for every simple coroot $h_{\alpha_j}$. 
On the other hand, the fundamental weights are defined by (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:fundamental_weights})
\begin{align}
    \omega_i(h_{\alpha_j})
    =\delta_{ij}.
\end{align}
Therefore,
\begin{align}
    \left(\sum_{i=1}^r\omega_i \right) (h_{\alpha_j})
    =
    \sum_{i=1}^r \delta_{ij}
    =1.
\end{align}
for every $j\in\{1,\ldots,r\}$. 
Since the simple coroots form a basis of the Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, the two functionals have identical values on a basis and hence coincide in $\mathfrak h^*$. 
Thus Eq.~\eqref{eq:delta_sum} follows.

Substituting the fundamental weight expansions of $\delta$ and $\Lambda$ from Eqs.~\eqref{eq:delta_sum} and \eqref{eq:highest_weight_expansion}, respectively, gives
\begin{align}
\label{eq:Lambda_delta_expand}
    2\langle\Lambda,\delta\rangle
    =2\sum_{i,j=1}^r\lambda_i\langle\omega_i,\omega_j\rangle .
\end{align}
It remains to express the inner products of fundamental weights, i.e., $\langle\omega_i,\omega_j\rangle$, in terms of the
Cartan matrix and the simple root lengths $\langle\alpha_j,\alpha_j\rangle$. 
Since the fundamental weights
$\{\omega_i\}_{i=1}^r$ form the basis dual to the simple coroots, each simple
root can be expanded as
\begin{align}
\label{eq:root_weight_relation}
    \alpha_i
    = \sum_{j=1}^r C_{ij}\omega_j ,
\end{align}
where $C_{ij}=\alpha_i(h_{\alpha_j})$ forms the Cartan matrix. 
Inverting this relation gives
\begin{align}
    \omega_i =\sum_{k=1}^r C^{-1}_{ik}\alpha_k.
\end{align}
Taking the inner product with $\omega_j$ and using Eq.~\eqref{eq:fundamental_weights}, we obtain 
\begin{align}
\label{eq:fundamental_inner}
    \langle\omega_i,\omega_j\rangle
    &=
    \sum_{k=1}^r C^{-1}_{ik} \langle\alpha_k,\omega_j\rangle \\
    &=
    \frac12 \sum_{k=1}^r C^{-1}_{ik} \langle\alpha_k,\alpha_k\rangle \delta_{jk} \\
    &=
    \frac12 C^{-1}_{ij} \langle\alpha_j,\alpha_j\rangle.
\end{align}
Equation~\eqref{eq:Lambda_delta_expand} therefore becomes 
\begin{align}
    2\langle\Lambda,\delta\rangle
    =\sum_{i,j=1}^r \lambda_i C^{-1}_{ij} \langle\alpha_j,\alpha_j\rangle,
\end{align}
this gives the claimed Cartan matrix expression for the lower bound and completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- mycor-15: body_md -->
{Optimal Lie Algebraic Uncertainty Relations}{Optimal_Lie_Algebraic_Uncertainty_Relations}
For an irreducible highest weight representation $V(\Lambda)$ of a compact semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbb R}$ and its complexification $\mathfrak{g}$ of rank $r$, the optimal state-independent lower bound on the Lie algebraic uncertainty is given by
\begin{align}\label{eq:Lie_Algebraic_UR_Optimal}
    \Delta^2_{\psi}(\mathfrak{g})
    \geqslant
    \vec{\lambda}^{\,\mathbf{T}}\cdot 
    C^{-1}\cdot
    \vec{\alpha},
\end{align}
where $\vec{\lambda}$ (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:Dynkin_Vector}) is the Dynkin coefficient vector, $\vec{\alpha}$ (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:Roots_Vector}) collects the squared simple root lengths, $C^{-1}$ denotes the inverse Cartan matrix (see Def.~\ref{def:Cartan_Matrix}).
<!-- end mycor-15 -->
<!-- mycor-16: body_md -->
{Simplified Lie Algebraic Uncertainty Relations}{Simplified_Lie_Algebraic_Uncertainty_Relations}
For an irreducible highest weight representation $V(\Lambda)$ of a complex simple Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ of rank $r$, the optimal state-independent uncertainty bound admits the expression
\begin{align}\label{eq:Lie_Algebraic_UR_Simplified}
    \Delta^2_{\psi}(\mathfrak{g})
    \geqslant
    \vec{\lambda}^{\,\mathbf{T}}\cdot 
    \vec{\xi}=
    \langle\underbrace{\vec{\lambda}}_{\text{Highest Weight}},\underbrace{\vec{\xi}}_{\text{Root System}}\rangle=
    \sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i\xi_i.
\end{align}
The vector $\vec{\lambda}$ collects the Dynkin coefficients of the highest weight $\Lambda$ (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:Dynkin_Vector}), while $\vec{\xi}=C^{-1}\vec{\alpha}$ contains the normalized root data (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:xi}).
Thus the bound depends on the highest weight, the root system, and the fixed metric. It is independent of the state within $V(\Lambda)$ and is attained on the highest weight group orbit.
<!-- end mycor-16 -->
<!-- mythm-9: body_md -->
{Simple Root Relabeling Invariance}{Simple_Root_Relabeling_Invariance}
The optimal state-independent bound in the Lie algebraic uncertainty relation is independent of the chosen ordering of the simple roots and, equivalently, of the labeling convention used for the Dynkin diagram.
<!-- end mythm-9 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Let $P$ denote the permutation matrix relabeling the simple roots. Under this relabeling, the Cartan matrix $C$ (see Def.~\ref{def:Cartan_Matrix}) and the vector $\vec{\alpha}$ (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:Roots_Vector}) of squared simple root lengths transform as
\begin{align}
    C'=P C P^{\dagger},
\end{align}
and 
\begin{align}
    \vec{\alpha'}
    =
    P\vec{\alpha}.
\end{align}
Consequently, the vector $\vec{\xi}$ (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:xi}) in the relabeled convention is given by
\begin{align}
    \vec{\xi'}
    =
    (C')^{-1}\vec{\alpha'}
    =
    (P C P^{\dagger})^{-1}P\vec{\alpha}
    =
    P C^{-1} P^{\dagger}P\vec{\alpha}
    =
    P\vec{\xi}.
\end{align}

The Dynkin coefficient vector $\vec{\lambda}$ (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:Dynkin_Vector}) is relabeled by the same permutation
\begin{align}
    \vec{\lambda'}
    =
    P\vec{\lambda}.
\end{align}
Hence, in the relabeled convention, the inner product between $\vec{\lambda'}$ and $\vec{\xi'}$ (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:Lie_Algebraic_UR_Simplified}) becomes
\begin{align}
    \langle\vec{\lambda'},\vec{\xi'}\rangle
    =
    (\vec{\lambda'})^{\mathbf{T}}\vec{\xi'}
    =
    (P\vec{\lambda})^{\mathbf{T}}
    (P\vec{\xi})
    =
    \vec{\lambda}^{\, \mathbf{T}}
    P^{\mathbf{T}}P
    \vec{\xi}
    =
    \vec{\lambda}^{\,\mathbf{T}}\vec{\xi}
    =
    \langle\vec{\lambda},\vec{\xi}\rangle.
\end{align}
Thus, the optimal value of the Lie algebraic uncertainty lower bound is invariant under simple roots relabeling.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- mylem-13: body_md -->
{Entries of $C^{-1}$ for Type-A Lie Algebras}{Inverse_Cartan_Matrix_A}
For the type-A Lie algebra $A_n$, the $(i,j)$-entry of the inverse Cartan matrix is
\begin{align}
\label{eq:An_inverse}
    C^{-1}_{ij}
    =
    \frac{\min\{i,j\}\,(n+1-\max\{i,j\})}{n+1}.
\end{align}
<!-- end mylem-13 -->
<!-- mylem-14: body_md -->
{Root Length Vector $\vec{\alpha}$ for Type-A Lie Algebras}{Root_Length_Vector_A}
For the type-A Lie algebra $A_n$, the squared simple root lengths form vector 
\begin{align}
\label{eq:An_Root_Length_Vector}
    \vec{\alpha}
    =
    \begin{pmatrix}
    2 \\
    2 \\
    \vdots \\
    2
    \end{pmatrix}.
\end{align}
<!-- end mylem-14 -->
<!-- mythm-10: body_md -->
{Components of $\vec{\xi}$ for Type-A Lie Algebras}{Root_Length_Vector_A}
For the type-A Lie algebra $A_n$, the components of the vector $\vec{\xi}$ (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:xi}) are
\begin{align}
    \xi_i=i(n+1-i),\quad \forall i\in\{1, \ldots, n\}.
\end{align}
<!-- end mythm-10 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Substituting the entrywise formula for $C^{-1}$ in Eq.~\eqref{eq:An_inverse} and the simple root length vector $\vec{\alpha}$ in Eq.~\eqref{eq:An_Root_Length_Vector}, the $i$-th component $\xi_i$ of $\vec{\xi}$ is obtained from the corresponding row sum. 
Splitting the sum into the two regions $j\leqslant i$ and $j>i$, we find
\begin{align}
    \xi_i
    &=
    \sum_{j=1}^{n}
    C^{-1}_{ij}\langle \alpha_j,\alpha_j\rangle\\
    &=
    \frac2{n+1}
    \left(
    \underbrace{\left(\sum_{j=1}^{i}
    j(n+1-i)
    \right)}_{j\leqslant i}
    +
    \underbrace{\left(
    \sum_{j=i+1}^{n}
    i(n+1-j)
    \right)}_{j>i}
    \right)\\
    &=
    \frac2{n+1}
    \left(
    (n+1-i)\frac{i(i+1)}2
    +
    i\frac{(n-i)(n-i+1)}2
    \right)\\
    &=
    i(n+1-i).
\end{align}
This establishes the desired expression and completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- mycor-17: body_md -->
{Type-A Lie Algebraic Uncertainty Relations}{Type_A_Lie_UR}
For the type-A Lie algebra $A_n$ (see Tab.~\ref{tab:Simple_Lie_Algebra}), the optimal Lie algebraic uncertainty relation (see Def.~\ref{def:Lie_Algebraic_Uncertainty_Relations}) takes the explicit form
\begin{align}
    \Delta^2_{\psi}(\raisebox{-0.6ex}{\includegraphics[scale=0.8]{DK_A_n.pdf}})\coloneqq
    \Delta^2_{\psi}(\mathfrak{sl}(n+1,\mathbb C))=
    \Delta^2_{\psi}(\mathfrak{su}(n+1))\geqslant
    \sum_{i=1}^{n}i(n+1-i)\lambda_i.
\end{align}
The bound is state-independent. 
It depends only on the representation, through the highest weight $\Lambda$ (see Subsec.~\ref{subsec:Highest_Weight_Representations}), or equivalently its Dynkin coefficient vector $\vec{\lambda}$ (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:Dynkin_Vector}), and on the type-A root system geometry encoded in $\vec{\xi}$ (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:xi}). 
Its optimality follows directly from the general result established in Cor.~\ref{cor:Simplified_Lie_Algebraic_Uncertainty_Relations}.
<!-- end mycor-17 -->
<!-- mylem-15: body_md -->
{Entries of $C^{-1}$ for Type-B Lie Algebras ($n\geqslant2$)}{Inverse_Cartan_Matrix_B}
For the type-B Lie algebra $B_n$ with $n\geqslant2$, the $(i,j)$-entry of the inverse Cartan matrix is
\begin{align}
\label{eq:Bn_inverse}
C^{-1}_{ij}
=
\begin{cases}
\min\{i,j\},
&
1\leqslant i,j\leqslant n-1,
\\[1.5ex]  
&
1\leqslant i\leqslant n-1,\quad\text{and}\quad j=n,
\\[1.5ex]  
\dfrac{j}{2},
&
i=n,\quad\text{and}\quad 1\leqslant j\leqslant n-1,
\\[2.5ex]  
\dfrac{n}{2},
&
i=j=n.
\end{cases}
\end{align}
<!-- end mylem-15 -->
<!-- mylem-16: body_md -->
{Root Length Vector $\vec{\alpha}$ for Type-B Lie Algebras ($n\geqslant2$)}{Root_Length_Vector_B} 
For the type-B Lie algebra $B_n$ with $n\geqslant2$, the squared simple root lengths form the vector 
\begin{align}
\label{eq:Bn_Root_Length_Vector}
    \vec{\alpha}
    =
\begin{pmatrix}
2 \\
\vdots \\
2 \\
1
\end{pmatrix}.
\end{align}
<!-- end mylem-16 -->
<!-- mythm-11: body_md -->
{Components of $\vec{\xi}$ for Type-B Lie Algebras ($n\geqslant2$)}{Root_Length_Vector_B}
For the type-B Lie algebra $B_n$ with $n\geqslant2$, the components of the vector $\vec{\xi}$ (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:xi}) are
\begin{align}
\xi_i=
\begin{cases}
       i(2n-i),\quad  &1\leqslant i\leqslant  n-1,\\[2ex]
       \dfrac{n^2}{2},\quad &i=n.
\end{cases}
\end{align}
<!-- end mythm-11 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
For $1\leqslant i\leqslant n-1$, the entrywise expression in Eq.~\eqref{eq:Bn_inverse} and the simple root length give
\begin{align}
    \xi_i
    &=
    \left(\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}
    C^{-1}_{ij}
    \langle\alpha_j,\alpha_j\rangle\right)
    +
    \left(C^{-1}_{i n}
    \langle\alpha_n,\alpha_n\rangle\right)
    \\
    &=
    2\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}
    \min\{i,j\}
    +
    i\cdot1 .
\end{align}
Decomposing the sum according to the two regimes $j\leqslant i$ and $j>i$, we obtain
\begin{align}
    \xi_i
    &=
    \left(2
    \underbrace{ \sum_{j=1}^{i}j}_{j\leqslant i}
    \right)+
    \left(2\underbrace{\sum_{j=i+1}^{n-1}i}_{j>i}\right)
      +
   \underbrace{i}_{j=n}
    \\
    &=
    2
    \left(
    \frac{i(i+1)}2
    +
    i(n-1-i)
    \right)
    +
    i
    \\
    &=
    i(2n-i).
\end{align}
Thus, for the interior indices $1\leqslant i\leqslant n-1$, 
\begin{align}
    \xi_i=i(2n-i).
\end{align}

It remains to consider the terminal short root node $i=n$, for which we use the final row of $C^{-1}$.

\begin{align}
    \xi_n
    &=
    \left(\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}
    C^{-1}_{n j}
    \langle\alpha_j,\alpha_j\rangle\right)
    +
    \left(C^{-1}_{n n}
    \langle\alpha_n,\alpha_n\rangle\right)
    \\
    &=
    \sum_{j=1}^{n-1}
    \frac{j}{2}\cdot 2
    +
    \frac n2\cdot 1
    \\
    &=
    \frac{n(n-1)}2
    +
    \frac n2\\
    &=
    \frac{n^2}{2}.
\end{align}
This proves the stated expressions and completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- mycor-18: body_md -->
{Type-B Lie Algebraic Uncertainty Relations ($n\geqslant2$)}{Type_B_Lie_UR_2}
For the type-B Lie algebra $B_n$ (see Tab.~\ref{tab:Simple_Lie_Algebra}) with $n\geqslant2$, the optimal Lie algebraic uncertainty relation (see Def.~\ref{def:Lie_Algebraic_Uncertainty_Relations}) takes the explicit form
\begin{align}
   \Delta^2_{\psi}( \raisebox{-1.4ex}{\includegraphics[scale=0.8]{DK_B_n.pdf}} )
   \coloneqq
   \Delta^2_{\psi}(\mathfrak{so}(2n+1,\mathbb C))
   =
   \Delta^2_{\psi}(\mathfrak{so}(2n+1))
   \geqslant
   \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}i(2n-i)\lambda_i\right)+
   \frac{n^2}{2}\lambda_n\,.
\end{align}
The lower bound is state-independent and is fixed entirely by representation-theoretic structure: 
the highest weight $\Lambda$ (see Subsec.~\ref{subsec:Highest_Weight_Representations}), or equivalently its Dynkin coefficient vector $\vec{\lambda}$ (see Eq.\eqref{eq:Dynkin_Vector}), together with the type-B root system geometry encoded in $\vec{\xi}$ (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:xi}). 
Its optimality follows directly from the general result established in Cor.~\ref{cor:Simplified_Lie_Algebraic_Uncertainty_Relations}.
<!-- end mycor-18 -->
<!-- mycor-19: body_md -->
{Type-B Lie Algebraic Uncertainty Relations ($n=1$)}{Type_B_Lie_UR_1}
For the type-B Lie algebra $B_n$ (see  Tab.~\ref{tab:Simple_Lie_Algebra}) with $n=1$, the optimal Lie algebraic uncertainty relation (see Def.~\ref{def:Lie_Algebraic_Uncertainty_Relations}) takes the explicit form 
\begin{align}
   \Delta^2_{\psi}( \raisebox{-0.6ex}{\includegraphics[scale=0.8]{DK_B_1.pdf}} )
   \coloneqq
   \Delta^2_{\psi}(\mathfrak{so}(3,\mathbb C))
   =
   \Delta^2_{\psi}(\mathfrak{so}(3))
   \geqslant
   \lambda_1\,.
\end{align}
The lower bound is state-independent and, in this rank-one case, is fixed entirely by the leading Dynkin coefficient $\lambda_1$ of the highest weight $\Lambda$ (see Subsec.~\ref{subsec:Highest_Weight_Representations}).
<!-- end mycor-19 -->
<!-- mycor-20: body_md -->
{Type-C Lie Algebraic Uncertainty Relations ($n=1$)}{Type_C_Lie_UR_1}
For the type-C Lie algebra $C_n$ (see  Tab.~\ref{tab:Simple_Lie_Algebra}) with $n=1$, the optimal Lie algebraic uncertainty relation (see Def.~\ref{def:Lie_Algebraic_Uncertainty_Relations}) takes the explicit form 
\begin{align}
\label{eq:Type_C1}
    \Delta^2_{\psi}( \raisebox{-0.6ex}{\includegraphics[scale=0.8]{DK_B_1.pdf}} )=
    \underbrace{\Delta^2_{\psi}(\mathfrak{su}(2))}_{\text{Type-A}}=
    \underbrace{\Delta^2_{\psi}(\mathfrak{so}(3))}_{\text{Type-B}}=
    \underbrace{\Delta_\psi^2(\mathfrak{sp}(1))}_{\text{Type-C}}
    \geqslant
    \lambda_1
    .
\end{align}
At rank one, the state-independent lower bound is fixed solely by the Dynkin coefficient $\lambda_1$ of the highest weight $\Lambda$; see Subsec.~\ref{subsec:Highest_Weight_Representations}.
<!-- end mycor-20 -->
<!-- mycor-21: body_md -->
{Type-C Lie Algebraic Uncertainty Relations ($n=2$)}{Type_C_Lie_UR_2}
For the type-C Lie algebra $C_n$ (see  Tab.~\ref{tab:Simple_Lie_Algebra}) with $n=2$, the optimal Lie algebraic uncertainty relation (see Def.~\ref{def:Lie_Algebraic_Uncertainty_Relations}) takes the explicit form 
\begin{align}
\label{eq:Type_C2}
    \Delta^2_{\psi}( \raisebox{-1.4ex}{\includegraphics[scale=0.8]{DK_C_2.pdf}} )\coloneqq
    \Delta_\psi^2(\mathfrak{sp}(2))
    \geqslant
    2\lambda_1+3\lambda_2
    .
\end{align}
For the rank-two case, i.e., $n=2$, the state-independent lower bound is fixed by the two Dynkin coefficients $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ of the highest weight $\Lambda$; 
see Subsec.~\ref{subsec:Highest_Weight_Representations}.
<!-- end mycor-21 -->
<!-- mylem-17: body_md -->
{Entries of $C^{-1}$ for Type-C Lie Algebras ($n\geqslant2$)}{Entries_Cinverse_Type_C}
For the type-C Lie algebra $C_n$, the $(i,j)$-entry of the inverse Cartan matrix is
\begin{align}
\label{eq:Cn_inverse}
    C^{-1}_{ij}
    =
    \begin{cases}
    \min\{i,j\},
    &
    1\leqslant i,j\leqslant n-1,
    \\[1.5ex]
    \dfrac{i}{2},
    &
    1\leqslant i\leqslant n-1, \quad\text{and}\quad j=n, 
    \\[2.5ex]
    j,
    &
    i=n,\quad\text{and}\quad 1\leqslant j\leqslant n-1,
    \\[1.5ex]
    \dfrac{n}{2},
    &
    i=j=n.
    \end{cases}
\end{align}
<!-- end mylem-17 -->
<!-- mylem-18: body_md -->
{Root Length Vector $\vec{\alpha}$ for Type-C Lie Algebras ($n\geqslant2$)}{Root_Length_Vector_C} 
For the type-C Lie algebra $C_n$ with $n\geqslant2$, the squared simple root lengths form the vector 
\begin{align}
\label{eq:Cn_Root_Length_Vector}
    \vec{\alpha}
